title: حِكَايَةُ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ
titleEn: The Lover and the Beloved, continued
part: Night 112 · The Lover and the Beloved, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 566–568 (Night 112, continuing directly from nights-111), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 112 continues the story that the vizier Dandān tells within the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, the story of the lover, the beloved and the go-between. Pressed by Tāj al-Mulūk, the young merchant draws out the scrap of cloth he has been hiding, weeps, and recites a poem of parting. Unfolded, the cloth shows two embroidered gazelles, one in silk and gold, the other in silver with a golden collar, and the prince asks for its story. The young man, whose name we now learn is ʿAzīz, begins: the only son of a great merchant, he was brought up with his cousin ʿAzīza, promised to him from childhood. The wedding is prepared, the guests invited for after the Friday prayer; fresh from the bath in a new perfumed suit, he turns down an unfamiliar lane to wait for the hour, sits sweating on a bench, and a white kerchief drops on him from above. He looks up, and his eyes meet those of the woman the gazelle belongs to. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّانِيَةَ عَشَرَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāniyata ʿashara baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the twelfth after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and twelfth night,
sentences.n: al-thāniyata ʿashara, “twelfth”: as on the night before, the print has the masculine عشر beside the feminine night; it is vocalised as printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الشَّابَّ قَالَ لِتَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ أَنَا مَا امْتَنَعْتُ مِنْ عَرْضِ بِضَاعَتِي عَلَيْكَ إِلَّا لِأَجْلِهَا فَإِنِّي لَا أَقْدِرُ أَدَعُكَ تَنْظُرُ إِلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-shābba qāla li-tāji al-mulūki anā mā imtanaʿtu min ʿarḍi biḍāʿatī ʿalayka illā li-ajlihā fa-innī lā aqdiru adaʿuka tanẓuru ilayhā
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the youth said to Tāj al-Mulūk: I — I did not refuse from displaying my merchandise to you except for its sake, for I am not able (that) I let you look at it.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the young man said to Tāj al-Mulūk, “It was only because of this that I would not show you my goods, for I cannot let you look at it.”
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the night by repeating the end of the one before. The print runs al-saʿīd and anna together (السعيدان), as it often does. li-tāji al-mulūki: li-, “to”, marking whom he speaks to. li-ajlihā, “for its sake”: li-, “for”, with ajl, “cause”. lā aqdiru adaʿuka, “I cannot let you”, without the an Classical Arabic puts before the second verb.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ لَا بُدَّ مِنْ كَوْنِي أَنْظُرُ إِلَيْهَا وَلَحَّ عَلَيْهِ وَاغْتَاظَ فَأَخْرَجَهَا مِنْ تَحْتِ رُكْبَتِهِ وَبَكَى وَأَنَّ وَاشْتَكَى وَأَكْثَرَ مِنَ الْأَنَّاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu tāju al-mulūki lā budda min kawnī anẓuru ilayhā wa-laḥḥa ʿalayhi wa-ightāẓa fa-akhrajahā min taḥti rukbatihi wa-bakā wa-anna wa-ishtakā wa-akthara mina al-annāti wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk said to him: There is no escape from my being (that) I look at it. And he pressed upon him and grew-angry; so he brought-it-out from under his knee, and wept, and moaned, and complained, and made-much of the moans, and recited these verses:
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk said, “I must look at it,” and pressed him and grew angry; so the young man drew it out from under his knee, weeping, moaning and lamenting, groaning again and again, and recited these verses:
sentences.n: lā budda min kawnī anẓuru, literally “there is no escape from my being I look”, a loose, spoken way of saying “I must look”. laḥḥa ʿalayhi, “he pressed him”, a spoken form of Classical alaḥḥa ʿalayhi. In the night before he hid the scrap under his thigh; here it comes out from under his knee — he is sitting on it. Rhymed prose: bakā, ishtakā; al-annāt, al-abyāt.

sentences.t:
لَا تَعْذُلِيهِ فَاِنَّ الْعَذْلَ يُوجِعُهُ * قَدْ قُلْتُ حَقًّا وَلٰكِنْ لَيْسَ يَسْمَعُهُ
اَسْتَوْدِعُ اللّٰهَ فِى الْبَطْحَاءِ لِي قَمَرًا * بِالْحَيِّ مِنْ فَلَكِ الْاَزْرَارِ مَطْلِعُهُ
وَدَّعْتُهُ وَبِوُدِّي لَوْ يُوَدِّعُنِي * صَفْوَ الْحَيَاةِ وَاِنِّي لَا اُوَدِّعُهُ
وَكَمْ تَشَفَّعَ بِي يَوْمَ الْفِرَاقِ ضُحًى * وَاَدْمُعِي مُسْتَهِلَّاتٌ وَاَدْمُعُهُ
لَا اَكْذَبَ اللّٰهَ ثَوْبُ الْعُذْرِ مُنْخَرِقٌ * عَنِّي بِفُرْقَتِهِ لٰكِنْ اُرَقِّعُهُ
لَا يَسْتَقِرُّ لِجَنْبِي مَضْجَعٌ وَكَذَا * لَا يَسْتَقِرُّ لَهُ مُذْ بِنْتُ مَضْجَعُهُ
وَقَدْ سَعَى الدَّهْرُ فِيمَا بَيْنَنَا بِيَدٍ * عَسْرَاءَ تَمْنَعُنِي حَظِّي وَتَمْنَعُهُ
وَصَبَّتِ الْهَمَّ صِرْفًا عِنْدَ مَا مَلَأَتْ * كَاْسًا تَجَرَّعَ مِنْهَا مَا اُجَرِّعُهُ
sentences.tr:
lā taʿdhulīhi fa-inna al-ʿadhla yūjiʿuhu * qad qultu ḥaqqan wa-lākin laysa yasmaʿuhu
astawdiʿu allāha fī al-baṭḥāʾi lī qamaran * bi-al-ḥayyi min falaki al-azrāri maṭliʿuhu
waddaʿtuhu wa-bi-wuddī law yuwaddiʿunī * ṣafwa al-ḥayāti wa-innī lā uwaddiʿuhu
wa-kam tashaffaʿa bī yawma al-firāqi ḍuḥan * wa-admuʿī mustahillātun wa-admuʿuhu
lā akdhaba allāha thawbu al-ʿudhri munkhariqun * ʿannī bi-furqatihi lākin uraqqiʿuhu
lā yastaqirru li-janbī maḍjaʿun wa-kadhā * lā yastaqirru lahu mudh bintu maḍjaʿuhu
wa-qad saʿā al-dahru fīmā baynanā bi-yadin * ʿasrāʾa tamnaʿunī ḥaẓẓī wa-tamnaʿuhu
wa-ṣabbati al-hamma ṣirfan ʿinda mā malaʾat * kaʾsan tajarraʿa minhā mā ujarriʿuhu
sentences.l:
Do not reproach him, (woman), for the reproach pains him; I have said truth, but he does not hear it.
I entrust to God in the stream-bed a moon of mine, in the encampment, from the orbit of the buttons its rising-place.
I bade-him-farewell, and in my wish (were it) that would bid-me-farewell the clearness of life, and that I do not bid-him-farewell.
And how-often he pleaded with me on the day of the parting, in the forenoon, and my tears pouring, and his tears!
No — I will not lie to God: the robe of the excuse is torn-open from me by parting-from-him; but I patch it.
There does not settle for my side a lying-place, and likewise there does not settle for him, since I went-away, his lying-place.
And the Time has worked between us with a hand left-handed, denying me my portion and denying him.
And it poured the care unmixed, when it filled a cup, from which he gulped what I make-him-gulp.
sentences.i:
Do not reproach him, woman, for reproach only hurts him; I have spoken the truth, but he does not hear it.
I leave in God’s keeping, there in the valley, a moon of mine, who rises among the tents from the circle of his collar.
I bade him farewell, and I would rather the sweetness of life had bidden me farewell, and I had never had to leave him.
How often he pleaded with me on the morning of our parting, my tears pouring down and his tears too!
God knows I do not lie: the robe of my excuses is torn by parting from him, but I patch it.
No bed will keep me lying still, and no more, since I left, will his bed keep him.
Time has meddled between us with a clumsy left hand, keeping my share from me and his from him,
a hand that poured out grief undiluted, filling a cup, and he drank from it the same draught as I.
sentences.n: The edition points this poem, and its pointing is kept. lā taʿdhulīhi speaks to a woman (“do not you, woman, reproach him”), the classic opening of a poem of parting. al-baṭḥāʾ is a broad stony stream-bed, the setting of desert love poetry. The “moon” is the beloved’s face, and its rising-place is “the orbit of the buttons” — his collar, from which his face rises like the moon over the horizon; bi-al-ḥayyi, “in the encampment”, bi- marking where. In line 3 the print points ṣafwa in the accusative; the sense is plain enough — he would rather lose life’s sweetness than lose him — and it is translated so. In line 5 the print points akdhaba, which would be a past tense; the line reads naturally as lā akdhibu allāha, “I will not lie to God”, an oath that what follows is true, and is translated so, with the print’s vowels kept. ʿasrāʾ, “left-handed”, is the unlucky, awkward hand. ujarriʿuhu, as pointed, is “I make him gulp”; the line is hard to construe exactly, but its sense is that both drink the same cup. The rhyme is -ʿuhu throughout.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ قَالَ لَهُ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ أَرَي أَحْوَالَكَ غَيْرَ مُسْتَقِيمَةٍ فَأَخْبِرْنِي مَا سَبَبُ بُكَائِكَ عِنْدَ نَظَرِكَ إِلَى هَذِهِ الْخِرْقَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha min shiʿrihi qāla lahu tāju al-mulūki arā aḥwālaka ghayra mustaqīmatin fa-akhbirnī mā sababu bukāʾika ʿinda naẓarika ilā hādhihi al-khirqati
sentences.l: And when he finished from his poetry, Tāj al-Mulūk said to him: I see your conditions not straight; so inform me, what is the cause of your weeping at your looking at this rag?
sentences.i: When he had finished his poem, Tāj al-Mulūk said to him, “I see that all is not well with you. Tell me, why do you weep when you look at this scrap of cloth?”
sentences.n: The print spells arā with a final ي (اري) rather than ى. khirqa is a rag, a scrap or piece of cloth.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الشَّابُّ ذِكْرَ الْخِرْقَةِ تَنَهَّدَ وَقَالَ يَا مَوْلَايَ إِنَّ حَدِيثِي عَجِيبٌ وَأَمْرِي غَرِيبٌ مَعَ هَذِهِ الْخِرْقَةِ وَصَاحِبَتِهَا وَصَاحِبَةِ هَذِهِ الصُّوَرِ وَالتَّمَاثِيلِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-shābbu dhikra al-khirqati tanahhada wa-qāla yā mawlāya inna ḥadīthī ʿajībun wa-amrī gharībun maʿa hādhihi al-khirqati wa-ṣāḥibatihā wa-ṣāḥibati hādhihi al-ṣuwari wa-al-tamāthīli
sentences.l: And when the youth heard the mention of the rag, he sighed and said: O my lord, my story is wondrous and my affair strange, with this rag and its owner (f.) and the owner (f.) of these pictures and the figures.
sentences.i: When the young man heard the cloth mentioned, he sighed and said, “My lord, mine is a wonderful story and a strange affair, with this scrap of cloth, and the woman it belongs to, and the woman these pictures and figures belong to.”
sentences.n: ṣāḥiba, literally “companion, owner” (f.), here the woman to whom the cloth belongs — and, as the tale will show, more than one woman is in play. Rhymed prose: ʿajīb, gharīb.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَشَرَ الْخِرْقَةَ وَإِذَا فِيهَا صُورَةُ غَزَالٍ مَرْقُومَةٌ بِالْحَرِيرِ مُزَرْكَشَةٌ بِالذَّهَبِ الْأَحْمَرِ وَقُبَالَهَا صُورَةُ غَزَالٍ آخَرَ وَهِيَ مَرْقُومَةٌ بِالْفِضَّةِ وَفِي رَقَبَتِهِ طَوْقٌ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ الْأَحْمَرِ وَثَلٰثُ قَصَبَاتٍ مِنَ الزَّبَرْجَدِ
sentences.tr: thumma nashara al-khirqata wa-idhā fīhā ṣūratu ghazālin marqūmatun bi-al-ḥarīri muzarkashatun bi-al-dhahabi al-aḥmari wa-qubālahā ṣūratu ghazālin ākhara wa-hiya marqūmatun bi-al-fiḍḍati wa-fī raqabatihi ṭawqun mina al-dhahabi al-aḥmari wa-thalāthu qaṣabātin mina al-zabarjadi
sentences.l: Then he spread-out the rag, and behold, in it (was) the picture of a gazelle embroidered with silk, brocaded with the red gold, and facing it the picture of another gazelle, and it embroidered with silver, and on its neck a collar of the red gold and three tubes of chrysolite.
sentences.i: Then he spread out the cloth, and on it was a gazelle embroidered in silk and worked with red gold, and facing it another gazelle, embroidered in silver, with a collar of red gold about its neck and three tubes of chrysolite.
sentences.n: wa-idhā, “and behold”, introduces what comes into view. bi-al-ḥarīr, bi-al-dhahab, bi-al-fiḍḍa: bi-, “with”, the thread the picture is worked in. “Red gold” is the stock phrase for the purest gold. qaṣabāt are small tubes or bugles, here of zabarjad, a green gem (chrysolite or peridot). The print writes thalāth with a dagger alif (ثلٰث).

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَظَرَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ إِلَيْهِ وَإِلَى حُسْنِ صَنْعَتِهِ قَالَ سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ الَّذِي عَلَّمَ الْإِنْسَانَ مَالَمْ يَعْلَمْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā naẓara tāju al-mulūki ilayhi wa-ilā ḥusni ṣanʿatihi qāla subḥāna allāhi alladhī ʿallama al-insāna mā lam yaʿlam
sentences.l: And when Tāj al-Mulūk looked at it and at the beauty of its making, he said: Glory of God, who taught the human what he did not know!
sentences.i: When Tāj al-Mulūk looked at it and saw how beautifully it was made, he said, “Glory be to God, who taught man what he did not know!”
sentences.n: ʿallama al-insāna mā lam yaʿlam is a phrase of the Qurʾān (96:5), said here in praise of the craftsmanship. The print runs mā lam together (مالم).

sentences.t: وَتَعَلَّقَ قَلْبُ تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ بِحَدِيثِ هَذَا الشَّابِّ فَقَالَ لَهُ احْكِ لِي قِصَّتَكَ مَعَ صَاحِبَةِ هَذَا الْغَزَالِ
sentences.tr: wa-taʿallaqa qalbu tāji al-mulūki bi-ḥadīthi hādhā al-shābbi fa-qāla lahu iḥki lī qiṣṣataka maʿa ṣāḥibati hādhā al-ghazāli
sentences.l: And the heart of Tāj al-Mulūk became-attached to the story of this youth, and he said to him: Tell me your tale with the owner (f.) of this gazelle.
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk’s heart was caught by this young man’s story, and he said to him, “Tell me your tale, and the tale of the woman this gazelle belongs to.”
sentences.n: taʿallaqa … bi-, “became attached to”: the verb takes bi- for what the heart hangs on.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ اعْلَمْ يَا مَوْلَايَ أَنَّ أَبِي كَانَ مِنَ التُّجَّارِ الْكِبَارِ وَلَمْ يُرْزَقْ وَلَدًا غَيْرِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu iʿlam yā mawlāya anna abī kāna mina al-tujjāri al-kibāri wa-lam yurzaq waladan ghayrī
sentences.l: And he said to him: Know, O my lord, that my father was of the merchants, the great ones, and he was not provided a child other than me.
sentences.i: He said to him, “Know, my lord, that my father was one of the great merchants, and he was blessed with no child but me.
sentences.n: lam yurzaq, “he was not granted”: rizq is what God provides, children among it.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ لِي بِنْتُ عَمٍّ تَرَبَّيْتُ أَنَا وَإِيَّاهَا فِي بَيْتِ أَبِي لِأَنَّ أَبَاهَا مَاتَ وَكَانَ قَبْلَ مَوْتِهِ تَعَاهَدَ هُوَ وَأَبِي عَلَى أَنْ يُزَوِّجَانِي بِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-kāna lī bintu ʿammin tarabbaytu anā wa-iyyāhā fī bayti abī li-anna abāhā māta wa-kāna qabla mawtihi taʿāhada huwa wa-abī ʿalā an yuzawwijānī bihā
sentences.l: And there was to me a daughter of a paternal-uncle; I was raised, I and her, in the house of my father, because her father died; and he had, before his death, made-a-pact, he and my father, on that they (two) marry me to her.
sentences.i: I had a cousin, my father’s brother’s daughter, and she and I were brought up together in my father’s house, because her father had died; and before his death he and my father had agreed that the two of them would marry me to her.
sentences.n: bint ʿamm, “daughter of a paternal uncle”, the cousin a man had the first claim to marry. tarabbaytu anā wa-iyyāhā, “I was raised, I and her”: the second party is tacked on with iyyā-, the free-standing object form, a common loose construction. yuzawwijānī is dual: “that the two of them should marry me”; bihā, bi-, “to her”, the preposition this verb takes for the bride.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا بَلَغْتُ مَبْلَغَ الرِّجَالِ وَبَلَغَتْ هِيَ مَبْلَغَ النِّسَاءِ لَمْ يَحْجُبُوهَا عَنِّي وَلَمْ يَحْجُبُونِي عَنْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā balaghtu mablagha al-rijāli wa-balaghat hiya mablagha al-nisāʾi lam yaḥjubūhā ʿannī wa-lam yaḥjubūnī ʿanhā
sentences.l: And when I reached the reaching-point of the men, and she reached the reaching-point of the women, they did not veil her from me and did not veil me from her.
sentences.i: When I came to manhood and she to womanhood, they did not keep her from me, nor me from her.
sentences.n: Grown cousins would normally be kept apart; they were not, because the two were promised to each other.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَحَدَّثَ وَالِدِي مَعَ أُمِّي وَقَالَ لَهَا فِي هَذِهِ السَّنَةِ نَكْتُبُ كِتَابَ عَزِيزٍ عَلَى عَزِيزَةَ وَاتَّفَقَ مَعَ أُمِّي عَلَى هَذَا الْأَمْرِ
sentences.tr: thumma taḥaddatha wālidī maʿa ummī wa-qāla lahā fī hādhihi al-sanati naktubu kitāba ʿazīzin ʿalā ʿazīzata wa-ittafaqa maʿa ummī ʿalā hādhā al-amri
sentences.l: Then my father talked with my mother and said to her: In this year we write the writ of ʿAzīz upon ʿAzīza. And he agreed with my mother upon this matter.
sentences.i: Then my father spoke with my mother and said to her, ‘This year we will draw up the marriage contract of ʿAzīz and ʿAzīza’; and he and my mother agreed on it.
sentences.n: This is the first time the young man’s name is given, in his father’s words: he is ʿAzīz, “dear, precious”, and his cousin is ʿAzīza. kataba al-kitāba ʿalā, literally “to write the writ upon”, is to draw up a marriage contract (katb al-kitāb, still the everyday phrase).

sentences.t: ثُمَّ شَرَعَ أَبِي فِي تَجْهِيزِ مُؤَنِ الْوَلَائِمِ هَذَا كُلُّهُ وَأَنَا وَبِنْتُ عَمِّي نَنَامُ مَعَ بَعْضِنَا فِي فِرَاشٍ وَاحِدٍ وَلَمْ نَدْرِ كَيْفَ الْحَالُ وَكَانَتْ هِيَ أَشْعَرَ مِنِّي وَأَعْرَفَ وَأَدْرَى
sentences.tr: thumma sharaʿa abī fī tajhīzi muʾani al-walāʾimi hādhā kulluhu wa-anā wa-bintu ʿammī nanāmu maʿa baʿḍinā fī firāshin wāḥidin wa-lam nadri kayfa al-ḥālu wa-kānat hiya ashʿara minnī wa-aʿrafa wa-adrā
sentences.l: Then my father began in preparing the provisions of the feasts; this all, and I and the daughter of my uncle sleeping with each-other in one bed, and we did not know how the state (was); and she was more-aware than me and more-knowing and more-understanding.
sentences.i: Then my father set about laying in provisions for the wedding feasts. And all this while my cousin and I slept side by side in one bed, knowing nothing of what was afoot, though she was quicker than I, and knew and understood more.
sentences.n: hādhā kulluhu, “all this (while)”, a loose spoken link. maʿa baʿḍinā, “with each other”, is Middle Arabic for the Classical maʿan. lam nadri kayfa al-ḥāl, “we did not know how things stood”: they were innocent of what was being prepared — though, he adds, she was the more knowing of the two. ashʿara, aʿrafa, adrā, “more aware, more knowing, more understanding”, a little run of comparatives on the same pattern (afʿal).

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا جَهَّزَ أَبِي أَدَوَاتِ الْفَرَحِ وَلَمْ يَبْقَ غَيْرُ كَتْبِ الْكِتَابِ وَالدُّخُولِ عَلَى بِنْتِ عَمِّي أَرَادَ أَبِي أَنْ يَكْتُبَ الْكِتَابَ بَعْدَ صَلٰوةِ الْجُمُعَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā jahhaza abī adawāti al-faraḥi wa-lam yabqa ghayru katbi al-kitābi wa-al-dukhūli ʿalā binti ʿammī arāda abī an yaktuba al-kitāba baʿda ṣalāti al-jumuʿati
sentences.l: And when my father prepared the implements of the joy, and there did not remain other than the writing of the writ and the going-in upon the daughter of my uncle, my father wanted to write the writ after the prayer of the Friday.
sentences.i: When my father had got everything ready for the wedding, and nothing was left but to sign the contract and for me to go in to my cousin, he decided to have the contract written after the Friday prayer.
sentences.n: faraḥ, “joy”, is also the everyday word for a wedding. al-dukhūl ʿalā, “going in to” the bride, is the consummation. The print writes ṣalāt as صلٰوة, the old Qurʾānic spelling with wāw and a dagger alif.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَوَجَّهَ إِلَى أَصْحَابِهِ مِنَ التُّجَّارِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ وَأَعْلَمَهُمْ بِذَلِكَ وَمَضَتْ أُمِّي وَعَزَمَتْ أَصْحَابَهَا مِنَ النِّسَاءِ وَدَعَتْ أَقَارِبَهَا
sentences.tr: thumma tawajjaha ilā aṣḥābihi mina al-tujjāri wa-ghayrihim wa-aʿlamahum bi-dhālika wa-maḍat ummī wa-ʿazamat aṣḥābahā mina al-nisāʾi wa-daʿat aqāribahā
sentences.l: Then he betook-himself to his companions of the merchants and others, and informed them of that; and my mother went and invited her companions of the women, and called her relatives.
sentences.i: Then he went round to his friends among the merchants and others and told them of it, and my mother went and invited her women friends and summoned her relations.
sentences.n: aʿlamahum bi-dhālika, “informed them of that”: the verb takes bi- for the news. ʿazamat, “invited”, is the spoken, Egyptian use of ʿazama; Classical ʿazama means “to resolve”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا جَاءَ يَوْمُ الْجُمُعَةِ غَسَلُوا الْقَاعَةَ الْمُعَدَّةَ لِلْجُلُوسِ وَغَسَلُوا رُخَامَهَا وَفَرَشُوا فِي دَارِنَا الْبُسُطَ وَوَضَعُوا فِيهَا مَايَحْتَاجُ إِلَيْهِ الْأَمْرُ بَعْدَ أَنْ زَوَّقُوا حِيطَانَهَا بِالْقُمَاشِ الْمُقَصَّبِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā jāʾa yawmu al-jumuʿati ghasalū al-qāʿata al-muʿaddata li-al-julūsi wa-ghasalū rukhāmahā wa-farashū fī dārinā al-busuṭa wa-waḍaʿū fīhā mā yaḥtāju ilayhi al-amru baʿda an zawwaqū ḥīṭānahā bi-al-qumāshi al-muqaṣṣabi
sentences.l: And when the day of the Friday came, they washed the hall, the prepared-one for the sitting, and washed its marble, and spread in our house the carpets, and put in it what the matter needs, after that they adorned its walls with the cloth, the gold-threaded.
sentences.i: When Friday came they washed the hall that had been made ready for the gathering, and washed its marble floor; they spread carpets through our house and set out in it everything the occasion needed, after hanging its walls with gold-threaded cloth.
sentences.n: qāʿa, the great reception hall of a Cairene house. li-al-julūs, li-, “for”, the sitting: the reception. The print runs mā yaḥtāju together (مايحتاج). muqaṣṣab, cloth worked with gold or silver thread.

sentences.t: وَاتَّفَقَ النَّاسُ عَلَى أَنْ يَجِيئُوا بَيْتَنَا بَعْدَ صَلٰوةِ الْجُمُعَةِ ثُمَّ مَضَى أَبِي وَعَمِلَ الْحَلْوِيَّاتِ وَأَطْبَاقَ السُّكَّرِ وَمَا بَقِيَ غَيْرُ كَتْبِ الْكِتَابِ
sentences.tr: wa-ittafaqa al-nāsu ʿalā an yajīʾū baytanā baʿda ṣalāti al-jumuʿati thumma maḍā abī wa-ʿamila al-ḥalwiyyāti wa-aṭbāqa al-sukkari wa-mā baqiya ghayru katbi al-kitābi
sentences.l: And the people agreed upon that they come (to) our house after the prayer of the Friday. Then my father went and made the sweets and the dishes of the sugar, and there did not remain other than the writing of the writ.
sentences.i: The guests had agreed to come to our house after the Friday prayer. Then my father went and had the sweetmeats made, and the dishes of sugar-work, and nothing was left but to write the contract.
sentences.n: yajīʾū baytanā, “come to our house”: jāʾa takes the place it comes to as a direct object, without a preposition. ḥalwiyyāt, “sweets”, is the spoken plural.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ أَرْسَلَتْنِي أُمِّي إِلَى الْحَمَّامِ وَأَرْسَلَتْ خَلْفِي بَدْلَةً جَدِيدَةً مِنْ أَفْخَرِ الثِّيَابِ فَلَمَّا خَرَجْتُ مِنَ الْحَمَّامِ لَبِسْتُ تِلْكَ الْبَدْلَةَ الْفَاخِرَةَ وَكَانَتْ مُطَيَّبَةً فَلَمَّا لَبِسْتُهَا فَاحَتْ مِنْهَا رَائِحَةٌ زَكِيَّةٌ عَبِقَتْ فِى الطَّرِيقِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad arsalatnī ummī ilā al-ḥammāmi wa-arsalat khalfī badlatan jadīdatan min afkhari al-thiyābi fa-lammā kharajtu mina al-ḥammāmi labistu tilka al-badlata al-fākhirata wa-kānat muṭayyabatan fa-lammā labistuhā fāḥat minhā rāʾiḥatun zakiyyatun ʿabiqat fī al-ṭarīqi
sentences.l: And my mother had sent me to the bath, and she sent after me a new suit of the finest of the clothes; and when I came-out from the bath I put-on that suit, the splendid-one, and it was perfumed; and when I put-it-on there wafted from it a fragrant scent that clung in the road.
sentences.i: My mother had sent me to the bathhouse, and sent after me a new suit of clothes, of the very finest. When I came out of the bath I put on that splendid suit; it had been perfumed, and as I put it on a sweet scent rose from it that filled the street.
sentences.n: badla, “a suit of clothes”, a later word. ʿabiqat, “clung, hung heavy”, of a scent that lingers. The print writes fī with a final ى (فى).

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ إِلَى الْجَامِعِ فَتَذَكَّرْتُ صَاحِبًا لِي فَرَجَعْتُ أُفَتِّشُ عَلَيْهِ لِيَحْضُرَ كَتْبَ الْكِتَابِ وَقُلْتُ فِي نَفْسِي أَشْتَغِلُ بِهَذَا الْأَمْرِ إِلَى أَنْ يَقْرُبَ وَقْتُ الصَّلٰوةِ
sentences.tr: thumma aradtu an adhhaba ilā al-jāmiʿi fa-tadhakkartu ṣāḥiban lī fa-rajaʿtu ufattishu ʿalayhi li-yaḥḍura katba al-kitābi wa-qultu fī nafsī ashtaghilu bi-hādhā al-amri ilā an yaqruba waqtu al-ṣalāti
sentences.l: Then I wanted to go to the mosque, and I remembered a companion of mine, so I turned-back searching for him, so-that he attend the writing of the writ; and I said in myself: I busy-myself with this matter until the time of the prayer draws-near.
sentences.i: Then, as I was about to go to the mosque, I remembered a friend of mine, and turned back to look for him so that he could be present at the signing; and I said to myself, ‘I will see to this until it is nearly time for prayer.’
sentences.n: al-jāmiʿ, the congregational mosque where the Friday prayer is held. ufattishu ʿalayhi, “searching for him”: the spoken use of fattasha ʿalā. li-yaḥḍura, li-, “so that”, with the subjunctive. ashtaghilu bi-, “busy myself with”: the verb takes bi- for the task.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنِّي دَخَلْتُ زُقَاقًا مَا دَخَلْتُهُ قَطُّ وَكُنْتُ عَرْقَانًا مِنْ أَثَرِ الْحَمَّامِ وَالْقُمَاشِ الْجَدِيدِ الَّذِي عَلَى جَسَدِي فَسَاحَ عَرَقِي وَفَاحَتْ رَوَائِحِي
sentences.tr: thumma innī dakhaltu zuqāqan mā dakhaltuhu qaṭṭu wa-kuntu ʿarqānan min athari al-ḥammāmi wa-al-qumāshi al-jadīdi alladhī ʿalā jasadī fa-sāḥa ʿaraqī wa-fāḥat rawāʾiḥī
sentences.l: Then I entered a lane I had never entered, and I was sweating from the effect of the bath and the new cloth that (was) on my body; so my sweat flowed and my scents wafted.
sentences.i: Then I turned into a lane I had never been down before. I was sweating from the bath and the new clothes on my back, so the sweat ran and my perfumes spread about me.
sentences.n: The print has روئحي, a misprint for روائحي, rawāʾiḥī, “my scents”, corrected here. ʿarqān, “sweating”, is a spoken form; the print declines it (عرقانا). Rhymed prose: sāḥa, fāḥat.

sentences.t: فَقَعَدْتُ فِي رَأْسِ الزُّقَاقِ لِأَرْتَاحَ عَلَى مَسْطَبَةٍ وَفَرَشْتُ تَحْتِي مِنْدِيلًا مُطَرَّزًا كَانَ مَعِي
sentences.tr: fa-qaʿadtu fī raʾsi al-zuqāqi li-artāḥa ʿalā masṭabatin wa-farashtu taḥtī mindīlan muṭarrazan kāna maʿī
sentences.l: So I sat at the head of the lane to rest on a bench, and spread under me an embroidered kerchief that was with me.
sentences.i: So I sat down at the top of the lane to rest on a stone bench, and spread under me an embroidered kerchief I had with me.
sentences.n: masṭaba, the stone or brick bench built against the front of a house. li-artāḥa, li-, “to”, of purpose. mindīl, a large kerchief or napkin.

sentences.t: فَاشْتَدَّ عَلَيَّ الْحَرُّ فَعَرِقَ جَبِينِي وَصَارَ الْعَرَقُ يَنْحَدِرُ عَلَى وَجْهِي وَلَمْ يُمْكِنِّي مَسْحُ الْعَرَقِ عَنْ وَجْهِي بِالْمِنْدِيلِ لِأَنَّهُ مَفْرُوشٌ تَحْتِي
sentences.tr: fa-ishtadda ʿalayya al-ḥarru fa-ʿariqa jabīnī wa-ṣāra al-ʿaraqu yanḥadiru ʿalā wajhī wa-lam yumkinnī masḥu al-ʿaraqi ʿan wajhī bi-al-mindīli li-annahu mafrūshun taḥtī
sentences.l: And the heat grew-severe upon me, and my forehead sweated, and the sweat began running-down on my face, and it was not possible for me the wiping of the sweat from my face with the kerchief, because it (was) spread under me.
sentences.i: The heat bore down on me, my forehead broke into sweat and it began to run down my face, and I could not wipe it away with the kerchief because I was sitting on it.
sentences.n: ṣāra yanḥadiru, “began to run down”: ṣāra with a present verb marks something starting. bi-al-mindīl, bi-, “with”, the instrument. The print marks the shadda of ʿalayya (عليّ).

sentences.t: فَأَرَدْتُ أَنْ آخُذَ فَرَجِيَّتِي وَأَمْسَحَ بِهِ وَجْنَتِي فَمَا أَدْرِي إِلَّا وَمِنْدِيلٌ أَبْيَضُ وَقَعَ عَلَيَّ مِنْ فَوْقُ
sentences.tr: fa-aradtu an ākhudha farajiyyatī wa-amsaḥa bihi wajnatī fa-mā adrī illā wa-mindīlun abyaḍu waqaʿa ʿalayya min fawqu
sentences.l: So I wanted to take my outer-robe and wipe with it my cheek; and I did not know except (that) a white kerchief fell upon me from above.
sentences.i: I was about to take my robe and wipe my cheek with it, when all at once a white kerchief fell on me from above.
sentences.n: The print has فرق, a misprint for فوق, fawqu, “above”, corrected here. farajiyya is a long, loose outer robe with wide sleeves. bihi, “with it”, is masculine though farajiyya is feminine: loose agreement, as often. fa-mā adrī illā wa-, “I knew nothing but that …”, the spoken way of saying something happened all of a sudden.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ الْمِنْدِيلُ أَرَقَّ مِنَ النَّسِيمِ وَرُؤْيَتُهُ أَلْطَفُ مِنْ شِفَاءِ السَّقِيمِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna dhālika al-mindīlu araqqa mina al-nasīmi wa-ruʾyatuhu alṭafu min shifāʾi al-saqīmi
sentences.l: And that kerchief was finer than the breeze, and the sight of it gentler than the healing of the sick.
sentences.i: That kerchief was finer than the breeze, and the sight of it sweeter than healing to the sick.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: al-nasīm, al-saqīm.

sentences.t: فَمَسَكْتُهُ بِيَدِي وَرَفَعْتُ رَأْسِي إِلَى فَوْقُ لِأَنْظُرَ مِنْ أَيْنَ سَقَطَ هَذَا الْمِنْدِيلُ فَوَقَعَتْ عَيْنِي فِي عَيْنِ صَاحِبَةِ هَذَا الْغَزَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-masaktuhu bi-yadī wa-rafaʿtu raʾsī ilā fawqu li-anẓura min ayna saqaṭa hādhā al-mindīlu fa-waqaʿat ʿaynī fī ʿayni ṣāḥibati hādhā al-ghazāli
sentences.l: So I took-hold-of it with my hand and raised my head to above, to look from where this kerchief fell; and my eye fell in the eye of the owner (f.) of this gazelle.
sentences.i: I caught it in my hand and looked up to see where the kerchief had fallen from, and my eyes met the eyes of the woman this gazelle belongs to.
sentences.n: The print again has فرق, a misprint for فوق, fawqu, “above”, corrected here. masaktuhu, “I took hold of it”, is the spoken form of Classical amsaktuhu. li-anẓura, li-, “to”, of purpose.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
sentences.n: The print sets the name as two words here, شهر زاد.
